title: When the Undertow Burns
premise: Kestrel Hartwell has spent twenty years tuning pianos in a coastal town, keeping her ears—and her past—closed. When dying linguist Maren Oduya, the last fluent speaker of Vessic, asks Kestrel to become her final student, Kestrel refuses, then can't stop hearing the language's cadences in the old houses she works in. Learning Vessic forces her to confront the fire at the Hartwell cannery that killed her father and was blamed on a man she knows was innocent—Maren's son, Tomas. As Maren fades, Kestrel must return to the burned site, recover the evidence she buried as a child, and choose between protecting her family's name and giving Tomas's memory justice. In the end she records Maren's last words, testifies at a reopened inquest, and finally buys the house she'd only ever rented from her own life.
about_author: Ines Whitlock is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent a decade transcribing small-town inquests along the Pacific coast before turning to fiction. Her work explores how ordinary people carry extraordinary secrets in the architecture of their daily lives.

chapters.title: The Tuning Fork Winter
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Kestrel: she tunes a dead widow's piano and hears, through the radiators, fragments of the house's past—a habit that keeps her at one remove from her own life. A letter arrives from Maren Oduya requesting 'one final student.' Kestrel burns it. Emotional beat: the comfort and cost of deliberate invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Working in the old Oduya house, she overhears Maren speaking Vessic to herself and is shaken—the cadence matches a lullaby her father sang before the cannery fire. She visits Maren under a pretext; Maren sees through it instantly. Emotional beat: the first crack in twenty years of silence.

chapters.title: A Language of Two Survivors
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Maren, who recounts losing her language community to the cannery collapse and her son Tomas to a wrongful conviction and prison death. She offers Kestrel lessons not as charity but as debt: 'You buried something on that point. I need it dug up.' Emotional beat: grief recognizing grief across an old wound.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Reluctant lessons begin; Vessic has no word for 'owner,' only 'keeper,' which unsettles her tenant-like existence. Flashbacks surface of the night of the fire—her father's ledger, her uncle's truck, her eleven-year-old self burying a tin box. Emotional beat: language as excavation.

chapters.title: The Uncle Who Paid for Silence
chapters.summary: Kestrel confronts her uncle Ray, now a respected town councilman, who assumes she wants money. He reveals just enough: the fire was insurance arson, her father discovered it, and Ray let Tomas take the blame to protect the family. Emotional beat: horror that the conspiracy wore a familiar face all along.

chapters.title: Tides Against the Point
chapters.summary: Maren's POV, weakening health. She teaches Kestrel the fire-song, a Vessic lament composed by cannery workers, and admits she chose Kestrel deliberately—she has known what the child saw since the funeral. Rising tension: Maren's doctor gives her weeks. Emotional beat: urgency braided with tenderness.

chapters.title: Return to Ash
chapters.summary: Kestrel returns to the cannery ruins at low tide and digs up the tin box: her father's ledger page proving Ray ordered the fire, plus her childhood testimony she was too frightened to give. Ray's men are watching the property. Emotional beat: terror transformed into resolve as she pockets the truth.

chapters.title: The Weight of a Name
chapters.summary: Ray offers Kestrel the family house outright if she stays silent; she realizes she has been 'a tenant' to him too. She refuses, but he threatens to expose her father's complicity in looking away. Climax approaches: she records Maren singing the fire-song as legal-adjacent testimony. Emotional beat: choosing justice over inheritance.

chapters.title: Inquest at Low Water
chapters.summary: Climax. At the reopened inquest, Kestrel presents the ledger, plays Maren's recording, and testifies in halting Vessic so the town must hear the language they helped kill. Ray collapses under cross-examination; the verdict posthumously clears Tomas. Emotional beat: public reckoning, costly and imperfect.

chapters.title: Keeper
chapters.summary: Resolution. Maren dies at dawn with Kestrel reciting the fire-song back to her—the language survives in one new mouth. Kestrel buys the small house she'd always rented, tunes its piano, and begins teaching Vessic words to neighborhood children. Emotional beat: quiet ownership of memory, home, and voice.
